brief.subject: IRS can now take card payments directly: final rules issued
brief.headline: IRS Finalizes Rules to Accept Card Tax Payments Directly
brief.dek: Final IRS card-payment rules, a new charitable break for standard-deduction filers, and proposed premium tax credit changes.
brief.lede: The IRS issued final regulations letting it accept credit and debit card tax payments directly, without routing taxpayers through third-party processors.

sections.heading: IRS cuts out card middlemen
bullets: Final regulations let the IRS take credit and debit card tax payments itself, without third-party payment processors.
The change implements Taxpayer First Act provisions, which could simplify how owners pay estimated and business taxes by card.
The rules also lift limits on the IRS paying fees under contracts tied to card tax payments.
The final rules do not say what card fees taxpayers will pay, so check before charging a large tax bill.

sections.heading: Charity break for non-itemizers
bullets: Beginning with tax year 2026, standard-deduction filers can also deduct qualifying cash gifts to charity.
Owners and freelancers who don't itemize should keep receipts for 2026 cash donations to claim the new deduction.

sections.heading: Premium tax credit rules may shift
bullets: Proposed IRS regulations would revise who qualifies for the premium tax credit and how it is calculated.
They would also change how taxpayers repay excess advance credit payments, a key issue for self-employed Exchange enrollees.
Anyone buying individual coverage through a Health Insurance Exchange for themselves or family could be affected.

sections.heading: Forgiven student debt taxable again
bullets: A tax exemption for forgiven student loans has expired, a study warns.
Borrowers, including owners and employees, could face an unexpected IRS bill on forgiven balances.
